source.title: Emergent inabilities? Inverse scaling over the course of pretraining
source.authors: James A. Michaelov; Benjamin K. Bergen

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. No apparent garbling or cutoff affects the study results.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures task accuracy across model sizes and pretraining checkpoints, rather than held-out cross-entropy loss or power-law fit. Its results bear on V6, downstream performance predictability.
record.gate_note: The paper tests accuracy on 12 downstream benchmark tasks across eight Pythia model sizes and eight training checkpoints. These results bear on V6 only; the study does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws to loss, or evaluate compute-optimal allocations. The text also discusses results from McKenzie et al. (2023b), but those cited results are not included as rows. Table 1 reports regression statistics aggregated over model-size/checkpoint observations; the figures show task results by model and checkpoint but are not numerically tabulated.
record.test_reason: The study measures downstream accuracy on 12 tasks across 8 Pythia sizes and 8 checkpoints. It regresses accuracy on log parameters, log tokens and their interaction (Table 1). On several tasks accuracy falls with scale and training, which bears directly on V6. It measures no loss, fits no power laws and tests no allocation or architecture, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find clear inverse scaling over training tokens on 5 of 12 tasks, and possible evidence on up to 8 in total. On those 5 tasks, larger models decline faster as training continues. Their main takeaway is that task performance is unstable during continued text pretraining, so models need regular re-evaluation.
record.recipe_differences: Measures benchmark task accuracy across model sizes and training checkpoints, using regression on log parameters, log tokens, and their interaction; it does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pattern varies by task and model size: five tasks show clear aggregate inverse scaling, while some declines are reported only for the largest model or models.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Exploratory study limited to eight Pythia model sizes and selected benchmark tasks already associated with inverse scaling. The authors note that model-specific idiosyncrasies may not generalize. Numerical checkpoint-level accuracies are presented in a figure rather than a table; regression results are aggregate task-accuracy associations and do not test loss scaling.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying reported results left out. The figure contains checkpoint-level accuracy traces, but exact values are not stated in the text and the aggregate regression results and text-described largest-model findings are recorded above.

untested.parts: Relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss. Downstream predictability on general or representative benchmarks: the tasks were preselected because they were already known to show inverse scaling with parameters. Scales beyond 12B parameters and 300B tokens.
Not tested: no held-out loss measured.
Not tested: no extrapolation of fits.
Not tested: no loss-law fits compared.

record.verdict_notes: The tasks were selected because they already showed inverse scaling with parameters. The challenges therefore show that V6 fails on adversarially chosen tasks, not that downstream scaling is generally unpredictable. Cited McKenzie et al. (2023b) results on Anthropic LMs are correctly excluded from rows. The regression is linear in log variables; the authors note that emergent nonlinearities would not be captured by it.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out cross-entropy loss and power-law relationships in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of power-law fits from small runs to larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their scaling with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
The study measures accuracy on selected benchmark tasks across parameters and training tokens, not broad downstream performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.
It does not test how loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with setup or fit choices; its exploratory accuracy regressions are not power-law fits to loss.
